item.text: {"chapter_id":"8B","judge_orientation":"The revised list freezes a broad, mixed program portfolio before testing execution: social transfers and poverty reduction, health access, austerity and fiscal management, labor policy, infrastructure and energy, pacification/security, institutional transformation, and international or climate commitments. It retains attributable implementation evidence, formal architecture, independent monitoring, adverse failures, contrary achievements, external shocks, and attribution limits. No score is assigned; moral approval or disapproval is not treated as effectiveness evidence.","entries":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0024-E007","reason_to_read":"Provides the clearest pre-period program baseline, including austerity, poverty reduction, pensions, wages, energy and food self-sufficiency, pacification, anti-corruption, macroeconomic stability, and international priorities.","role":"context","supported_lenses":["8B.1"],"corrected_summary":"The 2018 platform and governing project stated a broad portfolio including austerity, poverty reduction, pensions and wages, energy and food self-sufficiency, pacification, anti-corruption, macroeconomic stability, migrant protection, and international cooperation. It establishes goals, not their 2023 execution."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0048-E014","reason_to_read":"Adds a directly dated 2023 statement of the administration's social, environmental, climate, international, and disarmament commitments, preventing the portfolio from being reduced to domestic security and flagship projects.","role":"context","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"Mexico's September 2023 UN statement presented government commitments on poverty reduction, social programs, minimum wages, environmental sustainability, climate adaptation, peaceful dispute resolution, dialogue in Colombia and Venezuela, and nuclear disarmament. It establishes declared goals, not their implementation or outcomes."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E001","reason_to_read":"Links the stated pacification program to the institutional choice of a large, militarized National Guard and records the shift away from the promised withdrawal of armed forces from public security.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.2","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"AMLO's campaign and transition materials framed pacification around social causes and rejection of a frontal war, while the 2018-2024 plan created a 266-coordination National Guard and the administration soon emphasized militarization. The passage documents a strategic shift and institutional translation, not its complete causal explanation."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E001","reason_to_read":"Shows the scale and distribution of 2023 priority-program resources while preserving the warning that the comparison uses different program universes and budget is not delivery.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3"],"corrected_summary":"The 16 priority programs active in 2023 received 512,805 million pesos, over 40% of social-program spending; the pension increased sharply from 2020 to 2023 while the health-and-medicines program's charted allocation declined. The 2019 and 2023 program groups differ, and budget allocation alone does not establish service quality or presidential personal control."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0032-E006","reason_to_read":"Provides concrete favorable delivery evidence for a major social priority, while identifying its lagged period and limits on causation and durability.","role":"favorable","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3","8B.6","8B.7","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"From 2018 to 2022, the older-adult pension expanded from about 5 million beneficiaries receiving 580 pesos monthly to 10.8 million receiving 2,400 pesos; its 2022 exercised budget was 244,582.5 million pesos. This is lagged evidence of program scale and delivery, not by itself nationwide welfare causation, fiscal durability, or a full-year 2023 result."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0031-E008","reason_to_read":"Adds a directly applicable 2023 labor-policy implementation fact to the favorable side of the portfolio without claiming downstream effects.","role":"favorable","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.6","8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"CONASAMI's resolution raised the minimum wage by 20% from January 2023, to 312.41 pesos in the northern border zone and 207.44 pesos elsewhere. The passage establishes formal implementation, not effects on employment, inflation, distribution, or compliance."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E014","reason_to_read":"Balances the record with 2023 macroeconomic and investment context, identifies the administration's major priorities, and preserves external and alternative causes.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.2","8B.3","8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"The World Bank identifies the administration's emphasis on transfers, flagship infrastructure, the National Guard, the Isthmus corridor, Dos Bocas, energy self-sufficiency, and labor reforms; it reports 3.2% GDP growth in 2023 while noting low productivity and subdued investment. The passage does not establish that these outcomes were caused solely by presidential policy."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E002","reason_to_read":"Direct 2023 monitoring evidence tests whether priority programs had defined populations and results rather than merely large budgets.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.2","8B.6"],"corrected_summary":"In 2023, 13 of 16 priority programs identified their target population adequately, while three did not; the health-and-medicines program described its purpose as transferring resources rather than specifying a population and intended result. The findings concern program design, not proof that no services were delivered."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E004","reason_to_read":"Shows the material scale of programs classified as management rather than problem-oriented interventions and records that monitoring recommendations were disregarded to varying degrees.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.8"],"corrected_summary":"Four of 16 priority programs were classified in 2023 as Management because their central objectives did not clearly identify the public problem; they represented nearly 20% of the priority-program budget and did not measure results. CONEVAL also reported that monitoring recommendations had been disregarded to varying degrees, without identifying personal presidential direction."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E006","reason_to_read":"Offers a broad, independent implementation-quality check with both improvement and deterioration across programs, including the pension and health-related programs.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.6","8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"CONEVAL found in 2023 that 69% of priority programs had result-oriented purposes, 50% measured results adequately, and 38% had logical association requiring strengthening; two programs lacked such association. The pension had a CEM category of Destacado, while several programs improved or worsened across the 2020-2022 comparison. These are program-monitoring measures, not independent impact estimates."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0032-E003","reason_to_read":"Supplies the missing health-policy chain from institutional transition to worsened access, while preserving pandemic, measurement, and attribution alternatives.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"CONEVAL reports that health-access deprivation rose from 16.2% in 2018 to 39.1% in 2022 and associates the change with the Seguro Popular-to-Insabi transition, coordination problems, altered spending, pandemic effects, and measurement changes. It also describes the federal transition toward IMSS-Bienestar in the surrounding period; the evidence supports an adverse implementation outcome but not exclusive presidential causation."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E001","reason_to_read":"Shows that the administration had formal 2023 health rules, objectives, operating authority, and budget-linked implementation machinery, preventing missing outcomes from being mistaken for absent planning.","role":"favorable","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.6"],"corrected_summary":"The 2023 IMSS-BIENESTAR rules established a federal program for people without social security, free services, medicines and supplies, coordination structures, mandatory operation, and annual budget dependence. The instrument shows formal design and authority, not demonstrated service quality or nationwide results."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E004","reason_to_read":"Documents formal supervision, training, monitoring, corrective-action, evaluation, resource, and personnel mechanisms for the 2023 health program, while making clear that effectiveness was not demonstrated in the passage.","role":"qualifying","supported_lenses":["8B.3","8B.4","8B.5","8B.8"],"corrected_summary":"The 2023 rules required multidisciplinary supervision visits, written commitments, performance and quality review, corrective measures, evaluations, reporting, training, and administrative authority over resources and implementation. These are prescribed controls and capacities; the passage does not establish that they worked in practice."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E007","reason_to_read":"Tests resource mobilization and personnel fit in the security portfolio, including the military-civil spending shift, local-transfer reduction, National Guard growth, and certification gap.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3","8B.4","8B.5","8B.6"],"corrected_summary":"From 2019 to 2023, military institutions received 72.2% of security-institution spending; military spending rose 41.9% from 2018 while civil spending fell 50.8%, and federal transfers to states and municipalities fell 36%. National Guard personnel grew 51.9%, but 94% were military and 69% held the required police certificate. These figures show administration-level resource and staffing choices, not every presidential decision."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E008","reason_to_read":"Provides end-period operational proxies for whether National Guard expansion produced preventive and justice-system performance, with explicit limits on causal interpretation.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"From 2020 to 2023, local institutions accounted for 99.2% of prosecutor presentations and 98.5% of emergency calls, while the National Guard accounted for 0.8% and 1.5%; Guard presentations fell 71.4% from 2019 to 2023, confrontations rose 904.8%, and narcotics seizures fell 67.6%. These are performance proxies and do not alone prove effects on crime."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E011","reason_to_read":"Adds subnational comparative evidence testing whether the Guard strategy was associated with homicide reduction, rather than relying on national activity counts alone.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"Mexico Evalúa's 2019-2023 comparative analysis found that homicide reductions were not consistently associated with greater National Guard activity; in its controlled minimization, absence of Guard operations was the configuration associated with homicide reduction. The analysis does not prove that Guard operations increased violence everywhere or establish all causal alternatives."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0016-E009","reason_to_read":"Preserves mixed security outcomes and measurement uncertainty, including declines in some indicators, a 2022-2023 reversal, and doubts about homicide classification.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.7"],"corrected_summary":"The report records a 17.3% decline in homicide deaths between its comparison points and a 12% decline in reported crime per 100,000 inhabitants from 2018 to 2023, but a 15.9% crime increase from 2022 to 2023 and increases in some offenses. It also questions whether homicide reductions were counted consistently; the passage does not isolate presidential causation."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E015","reason_to_read":"Tests appointments, institutional staffing, and the distinction between executive and legislative responsibility.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.4","8B.5","8B.6"],"corrected_summary":"At the end of 2022, 25 high-level appointment processes were pending or delayed and only five had been filled; the report specifically documents Cofece's lack of quorum and a Supreme Court order concerning pending executive proposals. The aggregate vacancy count includes offices with different appointing authorities and does not assess every appointee's qualifications."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0026-E014","reason_to_read":"Provides direct 2023 evidence of appointment failure and later judicially compelled correction for IFT and COFECE, with narrower attribution than the critic's broader institutional claim.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.4","8B.5","8B.8"],"corrected_summary":"During the 2023 reporting period, the administration had left IFT and COFECE without functioning plenaries by not filling vacancies; after a Supreme Court order, López Obrador appointed three COFECE commissioners, while the IFT case remained pending. The passage supports an appointment and correction sequence, not a complete assessment of all autonomous bodies."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0026-E020","reason_to_read":"Documents the 2023 INAI quorum crisis, pending cases, executive-allied dissolution position, and subsequent judicial restoration, directly testing institutional durability and adaptation.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.5","8B.8","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"From March 2023 through the reporting period, INAI lacked the five-member quorum and had nearly 6,000 pending cases; the Senate did not appoint a commissioner, while López Obrador and allies supported dissolving the body. After the period, the Supreme Court allowed it to meet with four commissioners. This shows institutional impairment and judicial repair, not voluntary executive adaptation."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0012-E015","reason_to_read":"Captures the ruler's directly attributed electoral-reform objective, resource and staffing choices, public response to opposition, and the institutional resistance that tested the program.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.1","8B.2","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"In February 2023, López Obrador defended electoral reforms that would cut election funding, staffing, training, and some campaign-finance sanctions, arguing resources should be redirected to the poor, while disparaging large demonstrations against them. The article records proposals and rhetoric plus warnings about institutional risks; it does not establish that electoral manipulation occurred."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0013-E016","reason_to_read":"Provides the strongest independent account of Plan B's execution attempt, mass opposition, judicial suspension and invalidation, and the executive's response to institutional resistance.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.8","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"The administration pursued Plan B to shrink and weaken INE; large demonstrations and litigation followed, and the Supreme Court suspended and invalidated the reforms in May and June 2023 for legislative-procedure violations. The passage shows formal initiative, opposition, and judicial correction; it does not by itself establish effects on electoral outcomes."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0026-E017","reason_to_read":"Corroborates the 2023 mobilization and judicial invalidation from a separate institutional-freedom source, preserving contrary evidence that opposition and courts functioned.","role":"favorable","supported_lenses":["8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"Despite threats and manipulation, independent outlets and users mobilized against Plan B in February 2023, and the Supreme Court invalidated the reforms in May and June for legislative-procedure violations. This is evidence of functioning opposition and judicial checks, not evidence that the ruler voluntarily accepted them."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0055-E008","reason_to_read":"Provides authoritative constitutional review of the National Guard transfer and tests whether a central security implementation survived legal and institutional constraints.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"The Supreme Court held in 2023 that transferring the National Guard's administrative, budgetary, organizational, functional, and command control to Defense was unconstitutional because it conflicted with the Guard's constitutionally required civil-security attachment. The ruling concerns institutional structure and does not by itself establish individual officers' conduct."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0050-E010","reason_to_read":"Adds a directly observed 2023 crisis case with both substantial mobilization and reported distribution failure, while preserving the extraordinary external shock and incomplete recovery horizon.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.6","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"After Hurricane Otis, López Obrador deployed more than 10,000 troops and 1,000 government workers and promised aid, but AP reported that many poorer residents received little assistance amid shortages of food, water, fuel, medicine, and communications. The passage describes the early aftermath and does not assess the full reconstruction period or assign every delay personally to the president."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0031-E003","reason_to_read":"Supplies corroborating crisis-response deployment and delayed aid while documenting the storm's extraordinary intensity and the limits of presidential attribution.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"After Otis, residents reported waiting several days for aid; the government established a military and naval air bridge and deployed about 17,000 security personnel. The storm intensified unusually rapidly, and the source cannot attribute all delays to López Obrador or evaluate full recovery."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0030-E004","reason_to_read":"Tests flagship-project mobilization, deadline pressure, operational readiness, cost control, and end-period durability through directly observed partial opening and acknowledged uncertainty.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.3","8B.6","8B.7","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"In December 2023, López Obrador inaugurated only a partially completed 290-mile Maya Train section amid hours-long delays, an unfinished second track, and reported cost estimates rising from about 8.5 billion to as much as 28 billion dollars. He acknowledged missing work, uncertain exact construction cost, and a projected three-to-four-year period before operating costs might be covered; final audited cost and long-term benefits remained unresolved."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0040-E008","reason_to_read":"Adds audit-based evidence on financial substantiation, property documentation, and incomplete transfer to the Sedena-controlled company, strengthening the project-control and accountability test.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"An external audit of the 2023 public account reported more than 2.442 billion pesos in right-of-way expenditures awaiting substantiation and more than 5.684 billion pesos in property advances lacking completed ownership documents; the transfer from Fonatur to the Sedena-controlled company remained incomplete and deadlines were revised. The passage does not establish López Obrador's personal knowledge or the final recovery of funds."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0050-E005","reason_to_read":"Shows a late, directly attributed corrective intervention in medicine distribution while retaining the severe shortage baseline, preexisting constraints, and untested operational design.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"López Obrador's centralized medicine warehouse was intended to send unavailable medicines nationwide within 24 to 48 hours, using the armed forces or Birmex. AP reported unfilled prescriptions rising from 1.5 million in 2019 to 22 million in 2021 and about 12.5 million in 2022, while experts warned that centralization could create logistical risks; the excerpt does not show whether the promised system worked."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E013","reason_to_read":"Provides a broad independent mixed assessment: successful fiscal restraint and USMCA negotiation alongside centralized power, weakened checks, military expansion, and uneven policy results.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.3","8B.7","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"CSIS assessed the administration's policies as mixed, crediting restrained pandemic spending with avoiding a significant fiscal crisis and crediting successful USMCA negotiation, while describing military expansion, weakened independent checks, and adverse or counterproductive effects in several policy areas. It is an analytical assessment and does not isolate every causal pathway."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E016","reason_to_read":"Adds mixed fiscal and state-capacity evidence, including improved tax collection and manageable debt alongside uneven austerity, agency cuts, and durable military expansion into infrastructure.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.3","8B.6","8B.10"],"corrected_summary":"The review reports a higher tax-to-GDP ratio, manageable debt, and a balanced 2022 budget, but also a pandemic-era business loss, uneven agency cuts and centralization, and expanding military control of infrastructure and economic projects. It identifies both capacity gains and durability risks without proving that all effects were personally directed by López Obrador."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E015","reason_to_read":"Tests coordination, adaptation, continuity, and end-period progress across a substantial external implementation portfolio, while preserving the World Bank's partial scope and external shocks.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.9"],"corrected_summary":"At the 2023 midpoint review, eight of 24 World Bank partnership indicators were achieved, one partially achieved, five were on track, and ten were off track; implementation was affected by the pandemic, policy shifts, institutional turnover, security obstacles, cancellations, and restructurings. The government requested some changes or cancellations while policy lending and analytical support continued. This evaluates a World Bank portfolio, not the whole Mexican state."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0052-E020","reason_to_read":"Adds detailed contrary evidence of proactive restructuring and continued analytical engagement, preventing cancellations from being treated automatically as either failure or successful adaptation.","role":"qualifying","supported_lenses":["8B.6","8B.8"],"corrected_summary":"By December 2023, the World Bank portfolio had experienced closures, partial cancellations, dropped projects, unsigned loans, and several proactive restructurings to address bottlenecks. The record attributes these to changing priorities, budget limits, institutional and procurement constraints, and external context; it supports reassessment of methods but does not show that each change improved outcomes."}],"changes_from_draft":["Replaced the largely security-, pension-, health-outcome-, and Maya-Train-centered list with a portfolio-wide set covering the explicit program baseline, social policy, health, labor, fiscal capacity, infrastructure, security, institutions, international commitments, and crisis response.","Removed BATCH-0044-E010 as a stand-alone selection because the supplied passage establishes only that a security decree was issued and contains no substantive program content or execution evidence.","Retained BATCH-0032-E006 and BATCH-0031-E016 only with explicit lag and non-causation limits; added direct 2023 monitoring and implementation evidence around them.","Added independent and contrary evidence on program design, budget allocation, health rules, health supervision, appointments, electoral resistance, institutional repair, crisis response, procurement, World Bank implementation, fiscal management, and positive labor or macroeconomic developments.","Narrowed all summaries where reopened passages corrected dates, unsupported quantities, personal attribution, permanence, causal claims, or claims about demonstrated effectiveness.","Preserved adverse evidence without converting institutional failure, opposition, or outcomes into moral deductions from competence."],"unresolved_gaps":["Direct evidence connecting López Obrador personally to agency-level noncompliance, appointment delays, procurement weaknesses, and several implementation failures remains uneven.","The frozen portfolio has clearer program evidence than comparable end-period outcome evidence for energy self-sufficiency, food self-sufficiency, climate commitments, international initiatives, and some infrastructure projects.","Several outcome series are lagged to 2022 or combine pandemic, measurement, inherited-baseline, and external-shock effects; full-year 2023 attribution remains incomplete.","Formal health supervision, medicine-delivery, and correction mechanisms are documented, but their actual effectiveness and independence are not established.","The 2023 Otis evidence covers early response and distribution, not the full reconstruction trajectory.","Durability after the end of the period remains unresolved for pensions, health-system restructuring, military institutional roles, the Maya Train, and autonomous-body capacity."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["The revised list now spans many material program components, so the future judge should reopen the full ledger to test whether omitted evidence changes the breadth rule or reveals additional attributable implementation.","Several selected items are correlated or come from common monitoring frameworks; the full ledger should check source independence and avoid citation-counting.","The judge should revisit all outcomes after separating inherited capacity, pandemic and other shocks, subordinate initiative, measurement changes, judicial constraints, and realistic implementation lags.","The judge should specifically reopen the ledger for adaptation: whether monitoring findings, court decisions, project restructurings, health transitions, medicine procurement, and crisis-response failures produced documented changes in methods or personnel.","The judge should compare the selected adverse institutional evidence with any additional ledger evidence of functioning services, macroeconomic stability, labor implementation, international cooperation, and durable capacity before forming a chapter conclusion."]}
